title: 俞军产品方法论 (Yu Jun's Product Methodology)
author: 俞军 (Yu Jun)
description: Evaluate a product through user value, alternatives, and the conditions that make exchange worthwhile.
body:
## Products are exchanges, not feature lists

Yu Jun frames product management around the relationship between users, firms, and products. The publisher’s outline moves from those relationships to transaction models and decision-making. The useful shift is to ask what value changes hands, not simply what the team can ship. A user can like an idea and still have no reason to leave an existing solution.

## Make the alternative visible

A practical application is to write down the current workaround before evaluating the new experience. What does the user already get? What effort, risk, trust, or learning would switching require? This exercise is an application of the book’s exchange-centered framing, not a formula that guarantees adoption. Different users can face very different tradeoffs even when they see the same interface.

## Turn the model into a test

Choose one concrete user situation. Describe the existing behavior, the proposed benefit, and the cost of changing. Then observe whether the user actually makes the exchange. Keep the firm’s ability to sustain the service in view as well: a product must create value for the user without making continued provision impossible. Treat the model as something to revise with evidence, not a way to make intuition sound scientific.

title: The Crowd
author: Gustave Le Bon
description: Read a historically influential account of collective behavior critically, without treating its prejudices as settled psychology.
body:
## A group can change the conditions of judgment

Le Bon argues that a psychological crowd is not merely many people standing together. He describes a shared orientation in which suggestion, emotional contagion, and anonymity can change individual behavior. His account emphasizes the influence of vivid images, repeated assertions, and the prestige of leaders over sustained argument.

## Influence is not evidence

The lasting question is how a group comes to experience a claim as obvious. Repetition can make an assertion familiar; familiarity can be mistaken for confirmation. A confident speaker can coordinate attention without supplying new evidence. As a reading exercise, distinguish the content of a claim from the social conditions that make it persuasive.

## Read the book against its own assumptions

This is an influential nineteenth-century argument, not a reliable description of every crowd. Le Bon’s racial, gender, and class generalizations are prejudiced, and his sweeping claims should not be imported as modern scientific consensus. His framework can also miss cooperation, deliberation, and differences between institutions. Use it to generate questions about influence, then test those questions against observable behavior and contemporary research. Do not use “crowd psychology” as a shortcut for dismissing people who disagree with you.

title: Capital (Das Kapital)
author: Karl Marx
description: An introductory guide to Volume I: commodities, labor-power, and the organization of production.
sourceLabel: Marx/Engels Internet Archive: Capital, Volume I
body:
## Start with the commodity

This guide concerns Volume I, not every volume of Capital. Marx begins with the commodity and distinguishes its usefulness from the social relations expressed through exchange. He asks how a society organized around market exchange makes relations between people appear as relations between things. The argument is an analysis of a particular social system, not just a complaint about individual greed.

## Labor-power is not the same as completed labor

In chapters six and seven, Marx distinguishes the capacity to work, sold for a wage, from the labor performed during production. His explanation of surplus value depends on that distinction: the value produced during the working day can exceed the value represented by the wage. The analysis therefore turns toward control over production, the length of the working day, and how productivity gains are distributed.

## Keep explanation and endorsement separate

When reading, trace each term through the argument rather than translating every occurrence of “value” into market price. Ask what Marx is trying to explain, which assumptions carry the explanation, and where another economic account would disagree. His categories remain influential and contested; they should not be presented as uncontested economic laws. Terry’s original catalog marks this book as partially read, and that status is preserved here.

title: The Globalization Paradox
author: Dani Rodrik
description: Understand why deep economic integration can conflict with democratic choice and national policy autonomy.
sourceLabel: Harvard Kennedy School: author publication overview
body:
## Integration creates political choices

Rodrik challenges the idea that more global economic integration is always the right policy target. His central tension concerns democracy, national self-determination, and extensive economic globalization. Pursuing all three without limits can force a conflict over who gets to choose the rules.

## Ask who can change the rules

A useful way to apply this framing is to examine one policy disagreement. Which decisions are being standardized internationally? Which domestic choices become harder to reverse? Who benefits from predictability, and who loses the ability to adapt a rule to local preferences? These are analytical questions, not evidence that every international agreement is harmful.

## Distinguish globalization from its most demanding version

Rodrik’s argument is not a demand to end trade. It questions a model in which domestic institutions are continually reorganized around deeper integration. A more restrained international order can leave room for democratic variation. The practical reading task is to identify the tradeoff a proposal hides: do its promised economic gains require giving up a choice people still expect to make politically? Treat that tradeoff as something to debate openly, not a technical detail that experts have already settled.

title: The Great Divergence
author: Kenneth Pomeranz
description: Compare regions and constraints before explaining industrialization as an inevitable outcome of European superiority.
sourceLabel: Princeton University Press: description and table of contents
body:
## Compare like with like

Pomeranz asks why sustained industrial growth began in northwestern Europe. His comparison challenges stories that treat all of Europe and all of China as uniform units. The publisher’s account emphasizes similarities between advanced regions and the ecological constraints they faced before industrial divergence.

## Look for the constraint that changed

The book gives coal and access to resources from the New World a central role in explaining how parts of Europe escaped land-intensive limits. This is a change in the explanation: success cannot be read backward as proof that one region had always possessed every decisive advantage. Contingent access to energy and overseas resources matters alongside developments inside Europe.

## Do not turn a revision into a monocausal story

The practical lesson for reading historical arguments is methodological. Check the units being compared, the period under discussion, and the proposed causal mechanism. Similarity on one measure does not prove equality on every measure; the importance of coal does not make institutions irrelevant. Pomeranz’s account is an influential intervention in a continuing debate. Ask what evidence would distinguish a resource-constraint explanation from a claim that earlier cultural or institutional differences already made the outcome inevitable.

title: 台北人
author: 白先勇
description: A reading guide to memory, displacement, and the lives that continue after a historical rupture.
sourceLabel: Chinese University of Hong Kong Press / Columbia University Press
body:
## A collection, not one representative life

Pai Hsien-yung’s fourteen stories follow people whose lives in Taiwan remain entangled with memories of mainland China. The collection approaches displacement through distinct voices and social worlds. It does not reduce its characters to a single political argument or one model of nostalgia.

## Notice what the past does in the present

A useful reading question is not only what a character remembers, but what remembering allows them to do or prevents them from doing now. Social rituals, attachment, and self-presentation can keep an earlier identity alive even when the conditions supporting it have disappeared. This is an interpretive lens for reading, not a clinical diagnosis of the characters.

## Preserve the differences between stories

Compare how two characters respond to loss rather than extracting one moral from the collection. Who can tell their own story? Who is described by others? Where does sympathy coexist with irony? The value of the book is partly in these unresolved differences. Read slowly enough to notice voice and narrative distance; an overview can orient attention, but it cannot replace the experience of the prose.

title: 牡丹亭
author: 汤显祖
description: A reading orientation to Tang Xianzu’s drama of desire, dreams, and the authority of feeling.
sourceLabel: CUHK Renditions: Tang Xianzu and translated selections
body:
## Feeling becomes a dramatic force

The Peony Pavilion is Tang Xianzu’s celebrated drama, known in English through translations including Cyril Birch’s. Read it as a work of theater and lyric expression, not a modern argument with a single takeaway. Dreams and desire create a space in which experience can exceed the roles and expectations assigned to a person.

## Read for tensions, not just events

An interpretive starting point is the tension between inward conviction and outward authority. What makes an experience real to the person having it, and what would count as proof to a family or institution? Following that tension can make scenes more legible without collapsing their poetry into a lesson about individual freedom.

## Keep the performance in view

The page is only one way to encounter this work. Songs, pacing, gesture, and staging shape its effects. When a passage feels difficult, compare a translation with a responsibly contextualized performance rather than assuming that plot summary captures everything important. This short guide is an orientation, not a substitute for the drama or a scene-by-scene account. The linked scholarly material offers a starting point for identifying the author, translations, and selected passages.

title: Miyazakiworld
author: Susan Napier
description: Connect Miyazaki’s creative life with the recurring tensions in his films, rather than reducing them to comforting fantasy.
body:
## Biography and artistic worlds illuminate each other

Susan Napier examines Hayao Miyazaki’s life and work together. Yale’s overview highlights recurring concerns including women’s agency, environmental anxiety, and utopian imagination. The book provides a way to see relationships across films without assuming that every work communicates the same message.

## Look for a tension that remains unresolved

A productive viewing exercise is to choose one recurring theme and compare how two films handle it. Does technological wonder coexist with destruction? Does a place offer refuge while depending on hidden labor? These are suggested questions for interpretation, not a claim that every film contains the same symbolism.

## Resist the comfort of a single label

Calling the films simply environmentalist, nostalgic, or escapist can obscure the tensions that make them compelling. Attend to how an image makes conflicting feelings possible at once. Napier’s critical biography can supply context; a viewer still needs to test an interpretation against the film itself. Use the book to sharpen attention, not to replace watching with an approved explanation.

title: 耻
author: 【南非】J.M.库切
description: A critical orientation to power, responsibility, and the limits of self-understanding in Coetzee’s novel.
sourceLabel: Penguin Books: description and reader guide
body:
## A fall from status does not guarantee understanding

Coetzee’s novel follows David Lurie, a university professor whose involvement with a student costs him his position. He goes to stay with his daughter Lucy in rural South Africa. Their relationship is placed under further pressure by violence and by the unequal histories around them. The novel includes sexual violence and its aftermath.

## Separate a character’s account from the novel’s judgment

David’s ability to articulate a view does not make that view adequate. One useful reading discipline is to ask when his language clarifies an event and when it protects him from recognizing another person’s experience. Do not assume that access to his perspective amounts to endorsement by the author.

## Leave room for moral difficulty

This is not a clean redemption story or a practical manual for resolving political conflict. Its force lies in making responsibility, vulnerability, and authority difficult to separate. Track who can speak, whose choices David struggles to accept, and what changes in action rather than explanation. These questions are interpretive prompts; they should not flatten Lucy into a symbol or make one character stand for an entire society.
